tradeoff: The badges need a hover label to name themselves, and with Advanced on the sheet is 976 wide.

name: Stage Board Columns
idea: Workstreams as a calm stage board: four stage columns left to right (Needs you, Working, Idle, Ready to wrap up, with the Wrap Up rule inside Ready) and Leftovers as a shelf of four chips under the board; clicking a card widens its column while the others give way, and the card lists its agents, servers with small request-tick graphs, worktree and PR, caches and browser, then its actions with a preview of what goes and what stays. Performance shows ftop meters and apps by fate; Settings is written as sentences with words you can change.
good: You see every workstream's stage and holdings in one look, and the section button, Auto countdown, Undo and the Advanced mode fold-out all work.
tradeoff: The columns are narrow: when Working fills up it scrolls, and while a card is expanded the other columns cut long names short.

name: Stage Swimlanes
idea: Each stage is a horizontal lane read top to bottom, with two wide cards per row so long names fit and the marks sit on the right of each card; Leftovers is a fifth, quieter lane holding its rule and the Clean Up Leftovers button, and an expanded card takes the full lane width in two columns.
good: Names, states and sizes are never cut off, and the stages read like a short list from 'needs you' down to 'ready to wrap up', then leftovers.
tradeoff: It is taller per workstream, so when a new workstream arrives or a card is expanded the board scrolls.

name: Accordion Rows
idea: A 780 × 600 sheet with a three-word segmented control. Workstreams is grouped lists: Ready to wrap up first, with its Auto/Ask/Off chip and a live countdown in the group header, then Going, then Leftovers last. Each closed row shows its stage mark, name, live stage words, agent dots, a stacked bar of what it holds (servers, worktree, caches, browser) and its size. One row opens at a time into Agents (live, subagents arriving), Servers (mini heartbeat), Worktree and PR, and Caches and browser, each with its actions, plus a footer that says exactly what Wrap Up stops and removes. Advanced mode unfolds Agents, Servers, Worktrees and Disk into the same control while Performance turns into Apps.
good: It reads like one calm native list: closed, almost every workstream fits on one screen, and opening a row answers 'what does this hold and what does Wrap Up take' in place.
tradeoff: An open row is about 230 px tall, so the list below it scrolls, and only one workstream's anatomy shows at a time.
direction: Three tabs: rows that open in place

name: Row Poster
idea: The same rows sit in a 300 px list on the left; on the right, the picked row is laid out as a small poster: big name and live stage, the big 'held right now' number, a wide stacked bar, its action row, four labelled blocks (Agents with subagents as chips that come and go, Servers with heartbeats, Worktree, Caches with sizes), the Auto countdown and the Wrap Up footer. Leftovers becomes a memory map of blocks sized by GB. Performance, Settings and every Advanced tab use the same list and poster.
good: Every workstream gets a full, composed page that shows everything it holds and exactly what Wrap Up takes, while the list keeps the whole picture beside it.
tradeoff: The 300 px list trims stage words to one line, and a busy workstream like speed-3 fills the poster to its edge.
direction: Three tabs: rows that open in place

name: Day Lanes
idea: A 760 × 580 sheet with three segmented tabs. Workstreams is today drawn as one lane per workstream: who it is and where it runs; what it did since 9:00 (a bar while the agent works, a thin line while idle, white while it waits for you, a line under it for its servers, dots for its PR); a now line; a Next column that says live what happens next ('Asks you · Allow npm run build?', 'Ready 2 h · waits for your press', 'Auto wraps it up in 22 h'); and Holds. Leftovers are calm chips with 'Clean Up Leftovers · 31 GB'. Turning Advanced on unfolds Agents, Servers, Worktrees and Disk out of the tab bar one at a time, each with a glow in its own color.
good: Time explains the state: you see that fix auth redirect stopped at 14:42, its PR merged, and its 'ready' line has been waiting since 15:42; each lane answers what it is doing, what comes next and what it holds, and the setting sits in the column it controls.
tradeoff: Lanes are short (about 34 px), so long next-step text is cut at the column edge, and the morning part of the track is mostly empty.
direction: Three tabs: timeline or live map

name: Holdings Map
idea: Workstreams is a live map: each workstream is an island whose agent is a ring (breathing while it works, white when it waits), subagents orbit and pop in or fade out, and what it holds hangs off it on thin lines (servers that ripple on each request, a worktree with its PR, caches sized by GB, a browser). Ready islands get a dashed coral edge and their own Wrap Up button; Leftovers float unowned at the right edge as drifting bubbles with no lines. The star moment: turning Advanced on makes the holdings pour out as colored dots that arc through the sheet and land in Agents, Servers, Worktrees and Disk as those tabs unfold, each landing with a count.
good: Ownership is something you see (a line to an agent means it belongs to a workstream, no line means leftover), and the Advanced transition shows in one look what Advanced is: the same holdings lifted out into tabs of their own.
tradeoff: Each island has room for about four nodes, so busy workstreams fold servers into one node like ':3000 +1' and the details live in the hover card.
direction: Three tabs: timeline or live map

name: Faithful Poster
idea: 53-b Row Poster as drawn, corrected to the facts the 2.0 code has. A 300 px list of 14 workstreams on atlas, lexicon, studio and speed sits in Ready, Going and Leftovers. Each row has a Next sentence from facts, such as "Asks you · Allow npm run build?" or "Merged 2 h ago · Auto in 21 h". The picked row becomes a poster. Its big number is the disk Wrap Up frees, with memory as its own number. Below that come a disk bar, a memory bar, and the Session, Servers, Worktree and Caches blocks. The footer is the Wrap Up plan in run order: Servers, Helpers, Caches, Config, Worktree. Each part shows its title and size, and a blocked part shows its whyNot. The Advanced tabs use the same list and poster. They show agents with their why, servers with connections and a heartbeat of new connections, worktrees with git counts, and a disk map that counts APFS clones once.
good: The poster answers what the workstream is doing, what it holds and what Wrap Up takes, with no invented facts. Disk and memory are never added together. The plan lists every part in the order it runs, and Undo says it brings back the worktree and saved files and restarts its servers. Fifteen workstreams still read in the list.
tradeoff: The workstream poster is taller than the panel. On fix-auth-redirect the last plan parts and the Wrap Up button show only after you scroll, and a fade at the bottom edge is the only hint. Row Next sentences use short durations, and long session titles are cut with an ellipsis.

name: Plan first
idea: The poster leads with the Wrap Up plan as a checklist. Each part has its real title, the expert that runs it, and what it frees. A blocked part shows its whyNot with a lock. One live Next line above the plan says what the workstream is doing. The list holds 16 workstreams in Ready, Blocked, Going and Leftovers.
good: You see exactly what Wrap Up will take and what stops it before you press it. Disk and memory are two numbers, and the bar is disk only. The keep reasons follow MMWFWrapKeeps and MMWFWorkKeeps, so the Blocked group shows what the code would really say.
tradeoff: The plan pushes the agent and server facts below the fold, so a working workstream shows its checklist first. For an unmerged worktree the config and worktree parts both say "its branch is not merged", which is true to the code but less useful.

name: Twelve at once
idea: Row Poster at the scale the owner works at, with 15 workstreams across seven repos. The list groups rows by what each one needs from you: Asks you, Working, Ready to wrap up and Blocked, with Leftovers last. Each row is one 23 px line with a small live state. That state is the hook's question, the working time, the merge age or the whyNot, and next to it sits CPU for a working agent or the disk Wrap Up frees. The poster shows the session title and one Next sentence with its Go button. Below that are four fact lines (Agent, Servers, Worktree, Caches) and the five Wrap Up parts in plan order, each with its own unit and whyNot.
good: All 16 rows fit without scrolling, and the hook's question, the merge age and the whyNot read in full on the row. Every poster fits with no scroll, speed-3 with three servers included. Disk and memory always stay two numbers, and the plan shows Config even when it is empty. Undo restores the worktree and its saved files but never claims to restart a server.
tradeoff: The rows are dense. Waiting rows drop their CPU value to make room for the question, and subagents show only as dots on the row. The poster drops the per-block totals and the duplicate-server note to fit, so those live in the Servers and Worktrees tabs. Small blocks in the disk map cut their labels, and the full name sits in the hover card.

name: Faithful map
idea: 54-b Holdings Map with only the facts the code has. Each workstream is an island. A line is drawn only where a field links two things: an agent's cwd, a server's worktree or repoRoot, a cache's ownerPath, or a localhost tab on the server's port. A switch on the stage loads Quiet, Busy or Peak, and the stage panel shows live counts and says what the map gives up at Peak.
good: Browser nodes stay and show more. Chrome and Safari tabs sit on the server line for their port and glow while that browser is connected, and a headless helper is its own node. At Busy all 12 islands fit without scrolling. At Peak, over two minutes in headless Chrome, labels did not overlap, nodes stayed on their islands and frames held near 60 per second. The Wrap Up card lists the plan parts in order with each whyNot, and disk and memory are two separate numbers.
tradeoff: Peak does not fit in one view. The field scrolls past four rows, each island draws four holdings at most, servers merge into one node with a count, and each agent draws six subagent dots at most. Session titles are cut with an ellipsis at island width, and the full title is in the hover card. The tab-closing Wrap Up line is new, because no plan part closes tabs yet.
direction: Holdings Map with real facts, Quiet to Peak

name: Map at peak
idea: The holdings map built for Peak first. Islands pack into four bands by what they need from you: Asks you, Working, Ready and Blocked. The picked island and the ones that fit stay full size, and the rest shrink to rings with a count. Hovering a ring shows the island full size with its agents, servers, browser nodes, caches and helpers. Leftovers stay at the edge and merge into one bubble past six. A switch outside the sheet runs Quiet, Busy and Peak.
good: Peak stays readable at 60 fps with 20 workstreams, 28 agents, 35 servers, 60 localhost tabs and 25 leftovers. Labels do not overlap and no node sits off its island. Each server gets one browser node with an icon for each browser, and each icon glows while LocoHost lists that browser as a client. Wrap Up shows the plan parts in the code's order, with each whyNot and with disk and memory as two numbers.
tradeoff: At Peak only one island is full size, so ports, tabs and sizes need a hover. Ring names cut short at about eight letters. Islands move between bands as agents change state. Advanced lists scroll instead of fitting on one screen.
direction: Holdings Map with real facts, Quiet to Peak

name: Bento by holdings
idea: 58-a Faithful map laid out as a bento grid. Each workstream is one tile, and its size counts only what it holds: agents, servers, servers with localhost tabs, caches and helpers. Four holdings or fewer give a 1 x 1 tile with the name, the state and one line of colored counts. A 2 x 1 tile draws the 58-a node field with no merges. Anything bigger gets 2 x 2, with one row per server showing its port, framework and browser node. Tiles keep the fixture order and pack into two lanes, each tile into the shorter one. Leftovers are one tile at the right edge.
good: The workstreams with the most going on get the most room. speed-3-base shows all three servers with their tabs and its helper, and nothing merges. In two minutes of Peak in headless Chrome, no label overlapped another, no node left its tile, the grid had no holes and frames held at 61 per second. Tiles moved only when a holding changed. That happened at two Auto wrap ups and once when a server got its first tab, and then the tile grew from 1 x 1 to 2 x 1. The Wrap Up card and the Undo flow match the plan facts. Undo restarts the stopped servers and leaves helpers stopped.
tradeoff: The grid scrolls at Busy as well as at Peak, so 58-a's view of all 12 at Busy is gone. Tiles that ask you are not sorted to the top. A tile that asks can sit below the fold, and the header, the tab dot and the fold line point to it. Small tiles have no lines, and a question or session title in one is cut with an ellipsis, with the full text in the hover card. When one tile grows, the tiles after it repack, and a tile with no change of its own can move to the other lane. The tab-closing Wrap Up line is new, because no plan part closes tabs yet.
direction: Faithful map as a bento grid

name: Bento by need
idea: 58-a's map as a bento grid. A tile is 1 x 1, 1 x 2 or 2 x 2 from what the island holds. An island that asks you or is ready to wrap up gets one size step bigger. Ready tiles lead, and the other tiles keep a stable order.
good: What needs you is bigger. Big tiles draw every server, tab and cache with no merge, and add frameworks and a line of worktree facts. Small tiles keep quiet islands to one line of counts. Busy fits eight rows with no holes and no scrolling.
tradeoff: Need changes tile sizes. When an agent asks or is answered, its tile grows or shrinks and some nearby tiles glide. At Peak the field scrolls. Small tiles draw no nodes, and a tile can grow past its holdings to fill a cell.
direction: Faithful map as a bento grid

name: A bigger sheet
idea: 59-b's bento grid on a 1040 x 760 sheet. The grid has five columns of 183 x 94 cells, 16 px gaps and 16 px tile padding. Node labels are 11 px and tile text is 12 px. The scenario switch and the stage caption sit in a strip to the left, so the sheet still hangs from its icon. The Leftovers column is gone. Leftovers are one line under the grid, and its card lists every leftover.
good: Every label keeps 6 px to its node, to the next label and to the tile edge. Session titles and questions get their own line and are not cut. A tile keeps the size its holdings and need ask for, and legend tiles fill the cells left free. The leftovers line keeps disk and memory as two numbers, and its card gives each leftover its why, its size and its own action.
tradeoff: Fewer tiles fit in view. Busy shows 7 of 12 tiles, Peak about 7 of 20, and the field scrolls. A tall tile names a server by its port and counts its tabs. Five columns leave empty cells that legend tiles fill, sometimes three or more. The stage strip is narrow, so its Peak notes scroll.
direction: The bento grid with room to breathe

name: Show less per tile
idea: 59-b on the same 760 x 760 sheet, with three columns and fewer tiles in full. Each cell is 224 x 104 px, tiles have 16 px padding and the gaps are 14 px. Only an island that asks you, one that is ready to wrap up, and the one or two that hold the most get a 2 x 2 tile. A full tile shows the name and state, the question or session title on its own line, the node field with labels in fixed columns 21 px apart, and the worktree facts with Wrap Up or Answer in Tab. Every other island is a 1 x 1 summary with a name, a state and one line of counts. Hovering a summary, or clicking any tile, opens a card with the whole island and its Wrap Up plan in order. The Leftovers column is gone. Leftovers are one line under the grid, with chips for the biggest items, a count for the rest, Clean Up at the right end, and a card that lists every leftover with its why, size and action.
good: Nothing in a tile is cramped. In headless Chrome at Quiet, Busy and Peak, no label came within 6 px of another label or a node, and no node left its tile. Every session title and question fit on one line. Text in a tile is 12 px, captions and node labels 11 px. The grid had no holes and took the full width. In two minutes of Peak the frames held at 61 per second, with 17 ms as the longest frame. An ask that opens or closes a tile moves about four other tiles, and the opening tile stays near its old row. Both Auto wrap ups fired in the first minute. The Wrap Up card lists Servers, Helpers, the new Tabs line, Caches, Config and Worktree in order, and Undo restarts the stopped servers and leaves helpers stopped.
tradeoff: Most islands show no nodes, so you see their lines and browser tabs only in the card. About four rows show at once, so the grid scrolls at Busy too, and an island that asks can sit below the fold until the fold note and the header point to it. Tiles still open and close as agents ask and get answered, so the grid moves every few seconds at Peak. A full-width tile with only one or two holdings has a lot of empty space. To fill holes, a summary can grow to 2 x 1 or 1 x 2, and a tall summary shows its counts at the bottom with nothing above them.
direction: The bento grid with room to breathe

name: Mac Panel, Even
idea: An even 3 × 2 grid of six blocks (CPU and memory, Apps, Agents, Storage and leftovers, Servers, Network), each with a ring badge, a big number, five or six rows and one action, under a live insight line that names the biggest thing worth doing now with its button; the block it names gets a ring in its color, and Keep Awake is one checkbox line under the grid.
good: It reads like 01-a: the whole Mac on one calm sheet in the same place every time, and the line on top changes live (Clean Up Leftovers, then MinMacs Now, then Stop Idle Servers, then Offline).
tradeoff: Every block has the same size, so the block with the most to say shows only five rows plus 'N more'. Proposed facts: Down/up totals from interface counters; interface kind (Wi-Fi); volume size (994 GB), since MMPower has diskFree only.

name: Mac Panel, Weighted
idea: The same six blocks and insight line on a 3 × 3 grid: the block the line points at takes the top-left 2 × 2 with all its rows, a second column of detail and a note; the other five stay compact in fixed order, and blocks glide to new cells when the biggest issue changes (with a 7 s hold and a margin so it doesn't shuffle).
good: What matters most is also the largest thing on the sheet, with full detail where you act.
tradeoff: The compact blocks show only two rows each, and any change of focus moves the layout. Proposed facts: Down/up totals from interface counters; interface kind (Wi-Fi); volume size (994 GB).

name: Worth Doing First
idea: A ranked list of up to six actions leads the Performance tab, item 1 as the larger insight line with the primary button; a compact ftop meter row sits below (CPU with the agents' share and heat, memory with pressure, disk used and free, network), then three panels: Apps by fate, Storage and leftovers, Network and servers. Hovering an item dims the panels to the rows it touches and makes each bar's colored end exactly what it frees.
good: The page opens on a sentence and a button, and every number below it can be checked: hover an item and the meters and lists show exactly what it touches before you press.
tradeoff: The ranked list and meters take about half the sheet, so the three panels are short and scroll. Proposed facts: Interface down/up totals; route kind (Wi-Fi); a noise-tab rule and per-tab memory; npm/Docker/Simulators leftover fixtures.

name: Ranked With Detail
idea: The left column holds the ranked list and five This Mac rows (CPU, memory, disk, network, servers), with the lid checkbox at the foot; the right column becomes the detail of the row you hover: its bar, the rows it touches, its plan in run order with any reason a part is blocked, and its one button.
good: Each item gets a whole column to explain itself, including what Undo can and cannot bring back, and after an action the detail moves to the item that took its place.
tradeoff: One detail at a time, so comparing apps, storage and servers side by side takes several hovers. Proposed facts: Interface down/up totals; route kind (Wi-Fi); a noise-tab rule and per-tab memory; npm/Docker/Simulators leftover fixtures.

name: Zoomed disk bar
idea: Storage fills most of Performance: used and free as big numbers, the whole disk as one bar whose reclaimable end zooms out to full width, split By Kind or By Owner with gone owners ringed; each row opens to its items with Clean, Keep and Show in Finder, and Clean Up Leftovers previews the Trash part and the tool-command part. CPU, memory, apps by fate, network, servers and the lid checkbox sit in a quiet six-cell band whose cells open their detail above it.
good: It reads in one pass from 'how full is my disk' down to the exact items that can go and who left them, and it is honest that a Trash clean frees disk only when the Trash is emptied, while a tool's prune frees it at once with no Undo.
tradeoff: About five kinds show before scrolling, and CPU, memory, apps and servers are one hover away instead of on the page. Proposed facts: Disk total size from statfs (994 GB); whole-Mac down/up from interface counters. No per-app traffic.

name: Disk map
idea: A treemap of every disk item MinMacs knows: blocks sized by GB with clones counted once, grouped by kind, each labeled with its owner; gone owners ringed, running workstreams' caches as one dim group, the Trash as one block, report-only items hatched; Kind or Owner recolors the same layout, Clean Up Leftovers sits at the map's foot, and a quiet column on the right holds CPU, memory, apps, network, servers and the lid.
good: Who holds the disk shows at a glance, and cleaning reflows the map: what goes to the Trash visibly moves into the Trash block.
tradeoff: Small blocks lose their labels, so some need their hover card, and the map hides unsorted files behind one thin bar. Proposed facts: Disk total size from statfs (994 GB); whole-Mac down/up from interface counters. No per-app traffic.

name: Network as a band
idea: Top to bottom: a live insight line with its button, CPU and memory bars whose blue end is what MinMacs Now frees, a full-width network band (route and live total, local servers with connections now, the connected apps, memory and workstream, Stop Idle Servers, and what changes offline with the Keep Awake check), then apps by fate beside Storage with leftovers by kind and Clean Up Leftovers.
good: Network sits in the middle of the reading path and explains what the Mac is doing online (Safari and Chrome on :3000, Chrome for Testing on :5173); going offline changes the band, the insight and the keep-awake countdown live.
tradeoff: Four stacked rows fill the body, so the Kept apps scroll under a fade, and the band shows only the four busiest servers. Proposed facts: Live total down/up from interface counters; route kind (Wi-Fi); model reviews waiting while offline.

name: Network drawn live
idea: A small live diagram is the focal point: the Internet and the route out on the left, this Mac in the middle, servers with connections now as pills, the connected apps on the right; dots run along the route at a rate that follows the live total, and a dot runs from an app to its server for each new connection. Apps by fate sit below, meters and Storage in the right column.
good: You see the network as a picture of who talks to whom, every line backed by a fact, and it stays readable at Peak with 35 servers.
tradeoff: The diagram draws only the five busiest servers, and the narrow right column cuts Storage sub-lines short. Proposed facts: Live total down/up from interface counters (also sets the route dot speed); route kind (Wi-Fi); model reviews waiting while offline.

name: Bento by need
idea: Performance in 60-a's own bento language: tiles for CPU and memory, Apps, Agents, Storage and leftovers, Network, Servers and Keep Awake; each has a base size from what it holds, a tile with something worth doing grows one step and gets a tinted edge, the order stays put, and one insight line on the sheet head names the biggest thing worth doing, with its button.
good: Performance looks like the same product as Workstreams and tiles stay in place; when a tile is dealt with it shrinks while the insight line moves on to the next thing.
tradeoff: Because the order is stable, the most urgent tile can end up low in the grid, so the head line has to say what matters most. Proposed facts: Live down/up from interface counters; WorkForest pausing remote checks while offline; npm/Docker cache rows as tool rows and Simulators report-only.

name: Ranked bento
idea: The tiles re-rank live by what is worth doing: the top tile spans the full width and carries the insight line and its button, the rest follow by rank, and the change is calm (only when another tile beats it by an eighth, never twice within 4 s, with a 0.95 s glide).
good: What matters most is always the biggest thing at the top-left: going offline puts Network on top, a full disk puts Storage on top, and MinMacs Now hands the top to Servers.
tradeoff: Tiles move whenever the top pick changes, so you have to find a tile again. Proposed facts: Live down/up from interface counters; WorkForest pausing remote checks while offline; npm/Docker cache rows as tool rows and Simulators report-only.

name: Now and After
idea: A five-row ledger (CPU, Memory, Disk, Servers, Network) shows the Mac now, an arrow, the Mac after the ticked steps, and one sentence on what changes; MinMacs Now and Clean Up Leftovers are ticked by default, Wrap Up Ready and Stop Idle can be added; below, three panels (Apps by fate, Storage and leftovers, Network and servers) say what happens to each row: quits, to the Trash, runs its command, report only, with Wrap Up, or stays.
good: Every number has its after value: hovering a step lights what it touches, ticking a step moves the after column, and one button with a preview and one Undo runs the ticked steps.
tradeoff: The ledger takes about 40 % of the height, so the panels are short and scroll, and the steps row adds a choice to understand first. Proposed facts: Route kind (Wi-Fi); down/up rate from interface counters with a 60-sample sparkline; running a clutter row's cleanup command from Clean Up (MMClutterKind has cleanup and dryRun, no action runs them yet).
direction: Performance: now and after, or every size

name: Every size
idea: One ftop panel with ftop's own Compact, Medium and Large switch, and the sheet height follows (322, 600, 760 px): Compact is a strip of six ring meters under the insight line; Medium is 01-a's calm grid of six blocks, each with a badge ring, a big number, three rows and one action; Large keeps every block in place and lets each list everything (storage rows with owner, how it goes, the command and the trend; servers with workstream, connections and apps; agents' load; most memory per app).
good: The 1/117 panel made literal and smarter: the same blocks at three depths, the colored end of each bar is what MinMacs Now or Clean Up frees, and the insight line with its button stays on top at every size.
tradeoff: Large is Medium with more rows, not a new composition, and at Medium Storage hides most of its kinds. Proposed facts: Route kind (Wi-Fi); down/up rate from interface counters with a sparkline; a 60-sample CPU history in memory; running clutter cleanup commands.
direction: Performance: now and after, or every size

name: Three Panel Lift
idea: Under the ranked list and meters sit three even panels per tab: Agents has Ask you and working, Idle and why with ended sessions and where they run, and Load by workstream with the lid check. Servers has Busy now with a 30-minute heartbeat, Idle and recent with an idle bar and countdown to the rule plus the Off/Ask/Auto box, and Who connects with localhost tabs per browser, Docker and duplicates. Worktrees has Done or stuck, In a workstream, and Merged with no owner plus the rule. Disk has May go split Trash and own command, A workstream holds it, and Kept, blocked, report only plus the Leftovers rule.
good: Every fact the brief asks for has a labeled place on screen at once, and short lists get one extra line of real facts (started and last active, the Wrap Up parts, the commit at the head) so Quiet does not look bare.
tradeoff: At Busy and Peak the longest panel (working agents, busy servers, worktrees in a workstream) scrolls while its neighbours have room, and the narrow columns clamp secondary lines to two lines. Proposed facts: Subagent starts per sample kept in memory for an hour (the hooks report each start, and the code keeps only a count), drawn as the Agents meter sparkline and marked proposed on the page. Also used: the bind address shown as 'open to the whole network', and the localhost tab counts per server from MMMinMacsTab. Neither is proposed, both are in REAL-BRIEF.
direction: Lift: 120's own anatomy on every tab

name: Hero Graph Lift
idea: Under the ranked list and meters sit one wide hero graph and one narrow side panel. Agents: one lane per agent over the last hour, built from started, last active and the state now, with pink for working, white for asking, gray for idle, dots for subagent starts and ended sessions, beside Load by workstream and where they run. Servers: a heartbeat lane per server (one bar per minute of new connections), with idle stretches labeled and an idle bar to the rule's white mark with its countdown, beside Who connects and the rule. Worktrees: disk by fate as grouped bars, beside what the rule would and would never remove. Disk: the 994 GB disk zoomed into the known part by owner, then owner rows, beside the May go list, the rule and Clean Up.
good: Each tab gets one real graph that says in words what it means (timelines, heartbeat, the idle rule's countdown, disk by fate and by owner), and at Quiet the lanes and rows grow tall to fill the sheet.
tradeoff: The graph lanes are single-line, so some facts (dirty and unpushed details, per-agent CPU at Busy) move to hover or the side panel, and at Peak the hero and side panels scroll. Proposed facts: Subagent start times kept in memory for an hour, drawn as dots on the agent lanes and as the meter sparkline, marked proposed on the page. The lanes use only started and last active, so a pause inside a turn does not show, and the stage guide says so.
direction: Lift: 120's own anatomy on every tab

name: List and Detail
idea: Each tab has a 384 px list on the left with one row per item, grouped by state. When there is room, the rows grow to two lines and a summary fills the space under them: load by workstream, memory by workstream, disk by state or disk by kind. On the right, a detail fills the full height: header and actions, then one real graph that says in words what it shows, then a facts grid and two panels.
good: The detail answers everything about one item without any scrolling: an agent's question, CPU and memory with subagent starts, and its share of its workstream's load; a server's heartbeat with the idle stretch and the rule's mark drawn on the time axis, plus the tabs that show it; a worktree's counts, a timeline to the rule and what Wrap Up removes in plan order; a cache's size over 30 days and whether it goes to the Trash, by its own command or with a Wrap Up.
tradeoff: You see only one item's full story at a time. In Peak the list scrolls (21 of 28 agents and 21 of 34 servers fit), and the summary under the list shows only when Quiet or Busy leaves room. Proposed facts: An hour of CPU and memory samples per agent, kept in memory the way the Servers code keeps connections. A daily size per cache for the last 30 days. Both are marked proposed on the page. Agents starting and leaving in the sim come from session start and end, which the Worktrees code already has.

name: Detail Over Chips
idea: The picked item is a wide three-column card on top: header, facts and actions; the graph; and two panels, one being the rule with Off / Ask / Auto. Every item sits under it as chips in three balanced columns, grouped by state. The card shrinks to a floor of 312 px so the chips fit, and leftover room gets two side-by-side summaries.
good: The whole tab is visible at once, and Busy fits with no scroll on every tab (20 servers, 16 agents, 15 worktrees, 17 caches). The detail still carries the graph, the rule and the plan.
tradeoff: The card is shorter, so panels show less: Wrap Up shows its first 3 steps plus 'and N more', and a server shows only 2 tabs. In Peak the chips scroll (22 of 35 servers in view). Proposed facts: Same as 77-a: an hour of CPU and memory samples per agent, and a daily cache size for 30 days, both marked proposed on the page.

name: One Big Graph
idea: The sentence that matters and its button sit on top. The graph takes about two thirds of the sheet. Agents are swimlanes over the last hour, Servers are memory bubbles against idle time with the stop-after-2 h line and its chips, Worktrees are a field of trees by last-commit age and state, and Disk is a treemap by may go, held and kept. Under it are the 2 or 3 other actions with their sizes, plus the rule in plain Off / Ask / Auto words (or the lid check on Agents).
good: Every mark has its words beside it and a hover card with its actions, so you read the graph and act on it in one place. Hovering an action lights exactly what it touches on the graph, and its button previews the result before it acts.
tradeoff: At Peak the 28 agent bars need more rows than two thirds of the sheet holds, so the lanes scroll; lanes that ask you sort first and the clock axis stays put. Proposed facts: Agent state changes and the agents' CPU over the last hour, kept in memory while MinMacs runs (the code has only started, last active and the state now), shown as the bar history and a load strip marked proposed. Interface totals and route kind are inherited from 71-a.
direction: Lift: one big graph is the hero of each Advanced tab

name: The Graph Is the Tab
idea: The same four graphs fill the whole tab. The sentence that matters and its button become the graph's own headline. The actions and details live in hover cards and in a slim bottom bar, which holds the rule (Off / Ask / Auto in plain words, with its chips) and the 2 or 3 actions that fit.
good: The graph gets the most room, so Quiet looks full and Busy needs no scroll. Bubbles, trees and treemap cells are bigger, and their labels rarely drop.
tradeoff: The other actions are only one-line buttons in the slim bar, with no ranked list or why text, so you learn more by hovering. At Peak the last one or two agent lanes still scroll. Proposed facts: Same as 78-a: agent state history and the agents' CPU over the hour, kept in memory (proposed).
direction: Lift: one big graph is the hero of each Advanced tab

name: Even Fate Board
idea: Agents, Servers, Worktrees and Disk each open on one focal line with its button and a meter row that holds the rule or the lid checkbox, then 3 or 4 equal columns by fate (Asks you / Working / Idle, Busy / Idle / Kept or protected, Ready / Blocked / In a workstream / Stale, May go / Goes with Wrap Up / Kept). Each column header gives the count, the size and what happens to its cards, and a card that changes fate flies to its new column.
good: Columns always fill the sheet. Each column picks how much its cards show from the room it has: a poster with what the card touches (its workstream's holdings, the Wrap Up plan, the tabs on a port), a tall card, a full card, a compact card or a one-line card, so Quiet is not bare and Busy fits without scrolling.
tradeoff: Equal widths mean a crowded column folds to one-line cards while a sparse one beside it has spare room, and at Peak the Working, Busy and In a workstream columns scroll. Proposed facts: Network totals on the unchanged Apps tab as in 71-a; the Agents subagent bars count hook start events per 5 s over the last minute, kept in memory; Busy and Quiet start Stop idle servers on Ask (Peak on Auto), so orphans already past 2 h wait for a press instead of all being auto-stopped on load.
direction: Lift: columns by fate, like a board

name: Board by Share
idea: The same board, but each column is as wide as its share: of the cards on Agents and Servers, of the disk on Worktrees and Disk. The column that needs you (Asks you, Idle, Ready, May go) is always the widest, and widths animate as cards move.
good: What needs you gets the most room and the richest cards, so a question or the next thing to stop reads at a glance, and a big column can lay its cards out side by side.
tradeoff: Narrow columns get one-line cards and a few lines are cut short at Peak, and widths shift when shares change, so a column you were reading can move under the pointer. Proposed facts: Same as 79-a.
direction: Lift: columns by fate, like a board

name: Bento by Holdings
idea: Agents, Servers, Worktrees and Disk each group their items into workstream blocks plus one dashed No workstream block. The blocks are packed in rows, and each block's width and row height follow what it holds in that tab: agent count, server memory, worktree disk or cache disk. No block is ever smaller than its list needs, and spare room shows a live CPU-per-agent graph, a connections-per-hour graph, a caches-versus-checkout bar, a disk map or the Wrap Up plan.
good: Quiet and Busy fill the 1040 × 760 sheet with no scroll and no empty middles. Every block header links to its workstream and has its own action (Stop Servers, Wrap Up, Clean Up, Answer in Tab) with a hover preview, then Undo. The Servers graph shows each idle server sliding toward the 2 h rule line, with the countdown in words.
tradeoff: A block's size follows holdings, not urgency. A one-agent workstream that asks you can sit in a small block, and only the white dot and the top sentence make it stand out. At Peak the grid scrolls, and when four blocks must share a row, some second lines end in an ellipsis. Proposed facts: Each agent's CPU sampled every tick while MinMacs is open, kept in memory, drawn as 'CPU per agent, last 9 min'. Closing a workstream's localhost tabs as a Wrap Up line, carried over from 71-a and marked new. Network up/down rates, carried over from 71-a's Apps tab and marked proposed.
direction: Lift: each Advanced tab is a bento of workstream blocks that fills the sheet

name: Bento by Need
idea: The same blocks, but each block is sized and ordered by what it needs from you: an agent that asks, a server idle near or past the rule, a worktree ready or blocked. The biggest blocks sit top left. Blocks that need you get extra room: the agent's question in large type, an idle bar against the rule with its countdown, or the Wrap Up plan. Calm blocks shrink to one row and a count, or fold to just their header when room runs out.
good: What needs you is literally the biggest thing on every tab, and a block grows and moves to the top, animated, the moment its agent starts to ask. At Peak far more of the grid fits on screen than in 80-a.
tradeoff: Calm workstreams hide most of their items behind '+N more' or a folded header, so you hover the name to see them all. Blocks also move as needs change, so a block's position is less stable than in 80-a. Proposed facts: Same as 80-a: each agent's CPU sampled every tick and kept in memory (proposed), the closing of localhost tabs as a Wrap Up line (new, carried over from 71-a), and network rates (proposed, carried over from 71-a).
direction: Lift: each Advanced tab is a bento of workstream blocks that fills the sheet

name: Even Tile Grid
idea: Agents, Servers, Worktrees and Disk each open on a band (the sentence that matters and its button, three ftop meters, and the Off/Ask/Auto rule in plain words, or the lid check on Agents), then an even grid of tiles that fills the sheet. Each tile has a round badge with an arc gauge (agent CPU arc and state ring with subagent dots in its gap; server idle arc toward the rule's mark, with a ripple on each new connection; worktree and cache disk arc), a big number with a gray unit, and one plain line, sorted so what needs you comes first.
good: The grid picks 2, 4, 5 or 6 across so Busy fills the 1040 x 760 sheet with no scroll and no hole (a legend tile fills the free cells). Quiet tiles grow and show their facts and actions in place, so the sheet is never bare. Agents glow in when they arrive and say Finished before they fold away.
tradeoff: At Peak, 6 across makes small tiles about 150 px wide: the grid scrolls one or two rows, and long questions and session titles are cut to one line, with the full text in the hover card.
direction: Lift: a grid of ftop tiles, pure ftop

name: Two-Size Tile Grid
idea: The same band and tiles as 81-a, but what needs you (asks, idle servers, ready, blocked and merged worktrees, leftovers that may go) is a double 2 x 2 tile with its facts and actions in place, and so is the one that costs the most when there is room. The rest stay small and pack around them.
good: The one or two things to act on are the biggest things on the sheet, with their buttons right there (Answer in Tab, Wrap Up, Stop, Clean), while the grid still shows every item without scrolling in Busy.
tradeoff: Double tiles only appear while the grid fits four rows, so in Busy often only one or two get the big size (the costliest item drops first), and the small tiles are narrower than in 81-a; at Peak the grid scrolls.
direction: Lift: a grid of ftop tiles, pure ftop
